claim: About 300 loss-of-function mutations in the IKs channel have been identified in patients with Long QT syndrome and cardiac arrhythmia.
source: About 300 loss-of-function mutations in the IKs channel have been identified in patients with Long QT syndrome and cardiac arrhythmia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Hedley et al., 2009) and reference to a database (http://www.fsm.it/cardmoc/).

claim: Several Long QT syndrome-associated IKs channel mutations shift channel voltage dependence.
source: We find that several Long QT syndrome-associated IKs channel mutations shift channel voltage dependence and accelerate channel closing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Several Long QT syndrome-associated IKs channel mutations accelerate channel closing.
source: We find that several Long QT syndrome-associated IKs channel mutations shift channel voltage dependence and accelerate channel closing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Similar mutation-induced alterations in IKs channel currents may be caused by different molecular mechanisms.
source: Voltage-clamp fluorometry experiments and kinetic modeling suggest that similar mutation-induced alterations in IKs channel currents may be caused by different molecular mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp fluorometry data in Figure 3 and kinetic modeling in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: N-arachidonoyl taurine restores channel gating of many different mutant channels.
source: Finally, we find that the fatty acid analogue N-arachidonoyl taurine restores channel gating of many different mutant channels, even though the mutations are in different domains of the IKs channel and affect the channel by different molecular mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing N-AT effects on multiple mutants.

claim: N-arachidonoyl taurine restores function of mutant channels even though the mutations are in different domains of the IKs channel.
source: Finally, we find that the fatty acid analogue N-arachidonoyl taurine restores channel gating of many different mutant channels, even though the mutations are in different domains of the IKs channel and affect the channel by different molecular mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by data showing N-AT effects on mutations in different channel domains (Figure 1a, Figure 4).

claim: Most mutations causing LQTS are located in the KCNQ1 gene.
source: Most mutations causing LQTS are located in the KCNQ1 gene (Hedley et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hedley et al., 2009.

claim: KCNQ1 codes for the potassium channel KV7.1.
source: KCNQ1 codes for the potassium channel KV7.1, which in the heart co-assembles with the beta-subunit KCNE1 to form the slowly-activating, voltage-dependent potassium channel IKs (Barhanin et al., 1996; Sanguinetti et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barhanin et al., 1996 and Sanguinetti et al., 1996.

claim: KV7.1 co-assembles with the beta-subunit KCNE1 to form the slowly-activating, voltage-dependent potassium channel IKs.
source: KCNQ1 codes for the potassium channel KV7.1, which in the heart co-assembles with the beta-subunit KCNE1 to form the slowly-activating, voltage-dependent potassium channel IKs (Barhanin et al., 1996; Sanguinetti et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barhanin et al., 1996 and Sanguinetti et al., 1996.

claim: The IKs channel provides one of the important delayed rectifier outward potassium currents that repolarizes the cardiomyocyte and terminates the cardiac action potential.
source: The IKs channel provides one of the important delayed rectifier outward potassium currents that repolarizes the cardiomyocyte and terminates the cardiac action potential (Nerbonne and Kass, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nerbonne and Kass, 2005.

claim: Reduced IKs function tends to delay cardiomyocyte repolarization, thereby causing prolonged cardiac action potential durations and a prolonged QT interval.
source: Reduced IKs function therefore tends to delay cardiomyocyte repolarization, thereby causing prolonged cardiac action potential durations and a prolonged QT interval.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the role of IKs in repolarization.

claim: The cardiac IKs channel consists of four KV7.1 subunits and two to four KCNE1 subunits.
source: The cardiac IKs channel consists of four KV7.1 subunits and two to four KCNE1 subunits (Nakajo et al., 2010; Plant et al., 2014; Murray et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakajo et al., 2010; Plant et al., 2014; Murray et al., 2016.

claim: KV7.1 has six transmembrane segments named S1-S6.
source: KV7.1 has six transmembrane segments named S1-S6 (Liin et al., 2015) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liin et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: S1-S4 of each KV7.1 subunit forms a voltage-sensing domain where S4 is the voltage sensor with three positive gating charges.
source: S1-S4 of each KV7.1 subunit forms a voltage-sensing domain where S4 is the voltage sensor with three positive gating charges.
evidence: This is established knowledge about voltage-gated potassium channels.

claim: S5 and S6 from all four KV7.1 subunits form the pore domain with a putative gate in S6.
source: S5 and S6 from all four KV7.1 subunits form the pore domain with a putative gate in S6 that needs to move to open the ion-conducting pore of the channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about voltage-gated potassium channel structure.

claim: KCNE1 has a single-transmembrane segment.
source: KCNE1 has a single-transmembrane segment (Figure 1a) and is proposed to be localized in the otherwise lipid-filled space between two voltage-sensing domains of neighbouring KV7.1 subunits (Nakajo and Kubo, 2015).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1a and supported by citation to Nakajo and Kubo, 2015.

claim: KCNE1 is proposed to be localized in the lipid-filled space between two voltage-sensing domains of neighbouring KV7.1 subunits.
source: KCNE1 has a single-transmembrane segment (Figure 1a) and is proposed to be localized in the otherwise lipid-filled space between two voltage-sensing domains of neighbouring KV7.1 subunits (Nakajo and Kubo, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakajo and Kubo, 2015.

claim: Upon cardiomyocyte depolarization, the voltage sensor of KV7.1 moves outward in relation to the membrane.
source: Upon cardiomyocyte depolarization, the voltage sensor of KV7.1 moves outward in relation to the membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about voltage-gated channel function.

claim: The movement of the voltage sensor is transferred to the pore domain via the S4-S5 linker and induces channel opening by moving the S6 gate.
source: It has been proposed that this movement of the voltage sensor is transferred to the pore domain via the S4-S5 linker and induces channel opening by moving the S6 gate (Liin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liin et al., 2015.

claim: All KV7.1 and KCNE1 mutants except KV7.1/F193L+KCNE1 have a G(V) that is shifted towards positive voltages compared to the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channel.
source: When the KV7.1 mutants are co-expressed with KCNE1, all KV7.1 and KCNE1 mutants except KV7.1/F193L+KCNE1 have a G(V) that is shifted towards positive voltages compared to the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channel (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: KV7.1/F351A causes the most dramatic change by shifting V50 more than +30 mV.
source: KV7.1/F351A causes the most dramatic change by shifting V50 more than +30 mV.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1b and Supplementary file 1.

claim: V50 for KV7.1/S225L+KCNE1 is shifted almost +30 mV compared to wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1.
source: V50 for KV7.1/S225L+KCNE1 is shifted almost +30 mV compared to wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 (Figure 1c; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1.

claim: S225L slows down KV7.1+KCNE1 channel opening kinetics.
source: S225L also slows down KV7.1+KCNE1 channel opening kinetics (p<0.01; Figure 1d; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: All mutations, except for L251A, accelerate channel closing kinetics compared to wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1.
source: All mutations, except for L251A, accelerate channel closing kinetics compared to wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: K70N accelerates the closing kinetics by approximately a factor of 5.
source: K70N has the most dramatic effect on KV7.1+KCNE1 channel closing by accelerating the closing kinetics by approximately a factor of 5 (Figure 1e; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and Supplementary file 1.

claim: All mutants generate smaller currents than wild-type over a large voltage range.
source: When comparing the amplitude of K+ currents generated by these mutants with the current amplitude of the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channel in the same batch of oocytes, we note that all mutants generate smaller currents than wild-type over a large voltage range (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The reduced current amplitudes in Xenopus oocytes are mainly a result of gating defects (and not trafficking defects).
source: Although defective trafficking may contribute to these reduced currents in Xenopus oocytes, the current amplitudes for most mutants matches fairly well with the predicted current amplitude from channels with G(V) curves shifted towards positive voltages as observed for these mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a), suggesting that the reduced current amplitudes in Xenopus oocytes are mainly a result of gating defects (and not trafficking defects).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of observed and predicted current amplitudes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: F193L does not alter the G(V), but speeds up KV7.1+KCNE1 channel closing by a factor of 2.
source: F193L does not alter the G(V), but speeds up KV7.1+KCNE1 channel closing by a factor of 2 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Heterozygous expression generates channels with more wild-type like opening or closing kinetics and G(V) compared to homozygous expression of the mutant subunit.
source: Both of these examples show that heterozygous expression generates channels with more wild-type like opening or closing kinetics and G(V) compared to homozygous expression of the mutant subunit.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: A milder biophysical phenotype upon heterozygous expression is generally seen for the LQTS and LQTS-like mutants in terms of G(V), current amplitude, and/or closing kinetics.
source: A milder biophysical phenotype upon heterozygous expression is generally seen for the LQTS and LQTS-like mutants in terms of G(V), current amplitude, and/or closing kinetics (Figure 2c–d, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c-d, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The F(V) curve of KV7.1/G219C* correlates well with the G(V) curve.
source: As previously reported, the fluorescence versus voltage (F(V)) curve of KV7.1/G219C* correlates well with the G(V) curve (Figure 3a, left panel), while the F(V) curve of KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1 is divided into two components (Figure 3a, right panel) (Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Osteen et al., 2010; Osteen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and citations to Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Osteen et al., 2010; Osteen et al., 2012.

claim: The F(V) curve of KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1 is divided into two components.
source: As previously reported, the fluorescence versus voltage (F(V)) curve of KV7.1/G219C* correlates well with the G(V) curve (Figure 3a, left panel), while the F(V) curve of KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1 is divided into two components (Figure 3a, right panel) (Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Osteen et al., 2010; Osteen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and citations to Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Osteen et al., 2010; Osteen et al., 2012.

claim: For KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1, the first fluorescence component (F1) has been suggested to represent the main voltage sensor movement.
source: For KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1, the first fluorescence component (F1) has been suggested to represent the main voltage sensor movement and the second fluorescence component (F2) to be correlated with gate opening (Barro-Soria et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barro-Soria et al., 2014.

claim: For KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1, the second fluorescence component (F2) is correlated with gate opening.
source: For KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1, the first fluorescence component (F1) has been suggested to represent the main voltage sensor movement and the second fluorescence component (F2) to be correlated with gate opening (Barro-Soria et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barro-Soria et al., 2014.

claim: For KV7.1/G219C*/S225L, the F(V) curve is shifted to a similar extent as the G(V) curve.
source: For KV7.1/G219C*/S225L, the F(V) curve is shifted to a similar extent as the G(V) curve, while for KV7.1/G219C*/F351A, the F(V) curve is shifted to a considerably smaller extent (Osteen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and citation to Osteen et al., 2010.

claim: For KV7.1/G219C*/F351A, the F(V) curve is shifted to a considerably smaller extent than the G(V) curve.
source: For KV7.1/G219C*/S225L, the F(V) curve is shifted to a similar extent as the G(V) curve, while for KV7.1/G219C*/F351A, the F(V) curve is shifted to a considerably smaller extent (Osteen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and citation to Osteen et al., 2010.

claim: The S225L mutation primarily shifts F1 towards positive voltages so that F1 and F2 of KV7.1/G219C*/S225L+KCNE1 are hardly distinguishable in the F(V) curve.
source: The S225L mutation primarily shifts F1 towards positive voltages so that F1 and F2 of KV7.1/G219C*/S225L+KCNE1 are hardly distinguishable in the F(V) curve (Figure 3b, right panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b, right panel.

claim: The F351A mutation primarily shifts F2 towards positive voltages so that F1 and F2 are clearly separated.
source: In contrast, the F351A mutation primarily shifts F2 towards positive voltages so that F1 and F2 are clearly separated (Figure 3c, right panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c, right panel.

claim: S225L and F351A shift the G(V) curve of KV7.1+KCNE1 towards positive voltages by interfering with different gating transitions.
source: Thus, S225L and F351A seem to shift the G(V) curve of KV7.1+KCNE1 towards positive voltages by interfering with different gating transitions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different effects on F1 and F2 shown in Figure 3.

claim: The S225L mutation primarily interferes with the main S4 movement.
source: In summary, our voltage-clamp fluorometry experiments together with kinetic modeling are compatible with a model in which the S225L mutation primarily interferes with the main S4 movement, whereas the F351A mutation interferes with later gating transitions associated with pore opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on voltage-clamp fluorometry data in Figure 3 and kinetic modeling in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The F351A mutation interferes with later gating transitions associated with pore opening.
source: In summary, our voltage-clamp fluorometry experiments together with kinetic modeling are compatible with a model in which the S225L mutation primarily interferes with the main S4 movement, whereas the F351A mutation interferes with later gating transitions associated with pore opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on voltage-clamp fluorometry data in Figure 3 and kinetic modeling in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect of regular polyunsaturated fatty acids, such as docosahexaenoic acid, on KV7.1 is impaired by co-expression with the KCNE1 subunit.
source: We previously observed that the effect of regular polyunsaturated fatty acids, such as docosahexaenoic acid, on KV7.1 is impaired by co-expression with the KCNE1 subunit (Liin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liin et al., 2015.

claim: N-arachidonoyl taurine (N-AT) retained its ability to activate the KV7.1 channel also in the presence of KCNE1.
source: In contrast, we found that the PUFA analogue N-arachidonoyl taurine (N-AT, structure in Figure 4) retained its ability to activate the KV7.1 channel also in the presence of KCNE1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liin et al., 2015 and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: N-AT activated the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 by shifting the G(V) roughly –30 mV.
source: N-AT activated the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 by shifting the G(V) roughly –30 mV (Liin et al., 2015) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liin et al., 2015 and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 70 µM N-AT increases current amplitude by a factor of 16 at +20 mV for KV7.1/S225L+KCNE1.
source: 70 µM N-AT increases current amplitude by a factor of 16 at +20 mV (Figure 4a) and shifts the G(V) curve by about –50 mV (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 70 µM N-AT shifts the G(V) curve by about –50 mV for KV7.1/S225L+KCNE1.
source: 70 µM N-AT increases current amplitude by a factor of 16 at +20 mV (Figure 4a) and shifts the G(V) curve by about –50 mV (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Steady state of N-AT effects is reached within a few minutes.
source: Steady state of N-AT effects is reached within a few minutes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The human ventricular action potential has a duration of about 300–400 ms.
source: The human ventricular action potential has a duration of about 300–400 ms and a systolic voltage range of about 0 to +40 mV (O'Hara et al., 2011; Piacentino et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Hara et al., 2011 and Piacentino et al., 2003.

claim: The human ventricular action potential has a systolic voltage range of about 0 to +40 mV.
source: The human ventricular action potential has a duration of about 300–400 ms and a systolic voltage range of about 0 to +40 mV (O'Hara et al., 2011; Piacentino et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Hara et al., 2011 and Piacentino et al., 2003.

claim: The KV7.1/S225L+KCNE1 channel barely opens and thus generates only minor currents in response to repetitive 300 ms pulses to +40 mV at a frequency of 1 Hz and at 28°C.
source: In response to this protocol, the KV7.1/S225L+KCNE1 channel barely opens and thus generates only minor currents (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Large KV7.1/S225L+KCNE1 currents are observed upon application of 70 µM N-AT during repetitive pulsing.
source: In contrast, we observe large KV7.1/S225L+KCNE1 currents upon application of 70 µM N-AT (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: N-AT restores the gradual increase in current amplitude during repetitive pulsing seen experimentally and in computer simulations for the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channel.
source: N-AT also restores the gradual increase in current amplitude during repetitive pulsing seen experimentally (inset in Figure 4c) and in computer simulations (Silva and Rudy, 2005) for the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channel.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c inset and citation to Silva and Rudy, 2005.

claim: 70 µM N-AT shifts the G(V) curve of all tested mutants by 30–50 mV towards more negative voltages.
source: Further testing of N-AT show that 70 µM N-AT shifts the G(V) curve of all tested mutants by 30–50 mV towards more negative voltages (Figure 4d–e, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d-e and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The G(V) curve of wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 is shifted by –27.0 ± 2.5 mV by 70 µM N-AT.
source: The G(V) curve of wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 is shifted by –27.0 ± 2.5 mV (Liin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liin et al., 2015.

claim: 70 µM N-AT completely corrects the positive G(V) shifts induced by the mutations so that in the presence of N-AT the G(V) is similar to or shifted negative compared to the G(V) of the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channel.
source: Thus, 70 µM N-AT completely corrects the positive G(V) shifts induced by the mutations so that in the presence of N-AT the G(V) is similar to or shifted negative compared to the G(V) of the wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channel (Figure 4d, F351A homozygous expression was not included in this analysis because of the very shifted G(V) curve of this mutant).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: 70 µM N-AT reduces the energy required to open the channel by 5.3–9.0 kJ/mol depending on mutant.
source: 70 µM N-AT reduces the energy required to open the channel by 5.3–9.0 kJ/mol depending on mutant (4.9 ± 0.7 kJ/mol (n = 5) for wild-type) (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: 70 µM N-AT increases the current amplitude of all mutants at +20 and +40 mV.
source: 70 µM N-AT increases the current amplitude of all mutants at these voltages (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a–b, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4a-b and Supplementary file 3.

claim: 70 µM N-AT compensates fairly well (or overcompensates) for the mutation-induced reduction in current amplitude.
source: By multiplying these relative N-AT-induced increases in current amplitude with the relative current amplitude of each mutant (compared to wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channels, from Figure 1—figure supplement 4c–d), we observe that 70 µM N-AT compensates fairly well (or overcompensates) for the mutation-induced reduction in current amplitude (Figure 4g, Figure 4—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g and Figure 4—figure supplement 4c.

claim: For all mutant and wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channels, 70 µM N-AT speeds up the opening kinetics at +40 mV by a factor of 1.3–2.5.
source: Moreover, for all mutant and wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 channels, 70 µM N-AT speeds up the opening kinetics at +40 mV by a factor of 1.3–2.5 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: 70 µM N-AT slows down the closing kinetics for most mutants and wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1.
source: 70 µM N-AT also slows down the closing kinetics for most mutants and wild-type KV7.1+KCNE1 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: N-AT caused a dramatic decrease in the fluorescence from Alexa488-labeled KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1 channels.
source: Surprisingly, N-AT caused a dramatic decrease in the fluorescence from Alexa488-labeled KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1 channels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: N-AT did not decrease the fluorescence from Alexa488-labeled KV7.1/G219C* channels.
source: In contrast, N-AT did not decrease the fluorescence from Alexa488-labeled KV7.1/G219C* channels nor did high concentrations of taurine decrease the fluorescence from unbound Alexa488 (even up to concentrations of 0.5 M taurine; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that N-AT is not a collisional quencher of Alexa488.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: High concentrations of taurine did not decrease the fluorescence from unbound Alexa488.
source: In contrast, N-AT did not decrease the fluorescence from Alexa488-labeled KV7.1/G219C* channels nor did high concentrations of taurine decrease the fluorescence from unbound Alexa488 (even up to concentrations of 0.5 M taurine; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that N-AT is not a collisional quencher of Alexa488.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: N-AT is not a collisional quencher of Alexa488.
source: In contrast, N-AT did not decrease the fluorescence from Alexa488-labeled KV7.1/G219C* channels nor did high concentrations of taurine decrease the fluorescence from unbound Alexa488 (even up to concentrations of 0.5 M taurine; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that N-AT is not a collisional quencher of Alexa488.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that taurine does not quench unbound Alexa488.

claim: N-AT shifts both the voltage dependence of the first part (F1) and the second part (F2) of the F(V) curve towards more negative voltages for KV7.1/G219C*/S225L+KCNE1.
source: With this normalization, voltage clamp fluorometry experiments on KV7.1/G219C*/S225L+KCNE1 indicate that N-AT shifts both the voltage dependence of the first part (which represents F1) and the second part (which represents F2) of the F(V) curve towards more negative voltages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: For both mutants, 70 µM N-AT speeds up F1 kinetics.
source: For both mutants, 70 µM N-AT speeds up F1 kinetics (Figure 5a,d, measured at –40 mV where virtually no channels open and the fluorescence is mainly composed of F1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a,d and summarized in Figure 5f.

claim: N-AT accelerates the channel opening kinetics for KV7.1/G219C*/S225L+KCNE1 and KV7.1/G219C*/F351A+KCNE1.
source: Moreover, N-AT accelerates the channel opening kinetics (Figure 5b,e) and both the F1 and F2 fluorescence components at +80 mV for KV7.1/G219C*/S225L+KCNE1 (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b,e and summarized in Figure 5f.

claim: N-AT accelerates both the F1 and F2 fluorescence components at +80 mV for KV7.1/G219C*/S225L+KCNE1.
source: Moreover, N-AT accelerates the channel opening kinetics (Figure 5b,e) and both the F1 and F2 fluorescence components at +80 mV for KV7.1/G219C*/S225L+KCNE1 (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: N-AT accelerates both conformational changes during the main gating charge movement and channel opening.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that N-AT accelerates both conformational changes during the main gating charge movement and channel opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of N-AT on F1 and F2 kinetics shown in Figure 5.

claim: All studied LQTS and LQTS-like mutations shift the G(V) of KV7.1+KCNE1 towards more positive voltages, and/or accelerate KV7.1+KCNE1 closing.
source: We show that all studied LQTS and LQTS-like mutations i) shift the G(V) of KV7.1+KCNE1 towards more positive voltages, and/or ii) accelerate KV7.1+KCNE1 closing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: At least part of the mechanism underlying the reduced ability of these mutants to generate K+ currents is by altering the biophysical properties of the KV7.1+KCNE1 channel.
source: This suggests that at least part of the mechanism underlying the reduced ability of these mutants to generate K+ currents is by altering these biophysical properties of the KV7.1+KCNE1 channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed alterations in G(V) and closing kinetics.

claim: KV7.1/S225L primarily causes the reduced channel function by altering the main voltage sensor movement.
source: Our experimental data and kinetic modeling are consistent with a model in which KV7.1/S225L primarily causes the reduced channel function by altering the main voltage sensor movement, while KV7.1/F351A alters later gating transitions associated with pore opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on voltage-clamp fluorometry data and kinetic modeling shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: KV7.1/F351A alters later gating transitions associated with pore opening.
source: Our experimental data and kinetic modeling are consistent with a model in which KV7.1/S225L primarily causes the reduced channel function by altering the main voltage sensor movement, while KV7.1/F351A alters later gating transitions associated with pore opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on voltage-clamp fluorometry data and kinetic modeling shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The different effects of S225L and F351A on the fluorescence versus voltage relationships suggest that these mutations cause channel dysfunction via different molecular mechanisms.
source: The different effects of S225L and F351A on the fluorescence versus voltage relationships in KV7.1/G219C* and KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1 suggest that these mutations cause channel dysfunction via different molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different effects on F(V) shown in Figure 3.

claim: The current and fluorescence of the LQTS mutant F351L is very similar to the current and fluorescence of F351A.
source: However, during the review process of this manuscript a new LQTS mutation, F351L, was found (Vyas et al., 2016). The current and fluorescence of this LQTS mutant is very similar to the current and fluorescence of F351A (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting that our conclusions on the LQTS-like F351A is also relevant for the LQTS mutant F351L.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and citation to Vyas et al., 2016.

claim: Heterozygous expression of mutated subunits and wild-type subunits in equal molar ratios results in general in a milder biophysical phenotype.
source: Heterozygous expression of mutated subunits and wild-type subunits in equal molar ratios results in general in a milder biophysical phenotype (more close to the wild-type phenotype).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A milder clinical phenotype is generally reported for heterozygous carriers of LQTS mutations compared to individuals with homozygous genotypes.
source: This is in line with a milder clinical phenotype generally reported for heterozygous carriers of LQTS mutations compared to individuals with homozygous genotypes (Priori et al., 1998; Jackson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Priori et al., 1998; Jackson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: All tested mutants respond to N-AT.
source: Our results show that all tested mutants respond to N-AT.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutants show markedly different sensitivity to previously reported KV7 channel activators.
source: This is in contrast to previously reported KV7 channel activators on disease-causing KV7 mutants, for which mutants show markedly different sensitivity (Seebohm et al., 2003; Xiong et al., 2007; Leitner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seebohm et al., 2003; Xiong et al., 2007; Leitner et al., 2012.

claim: N-AT is an interesting model compound for development of future anti-arrhythmics to treat LQTS caused by diverse KV7.1+KCNE1 mutations.
source: This general ability of N-AT to, at least partly, compensate for the reduced function of mutants with mutations in different parts of the KV7.1+KCNE1 channel complex and with seemingly different molecular defects, as long as a population of these mutant channels reaches the plasma membrane, suggests that N-AT is an interesting model compound for development of future anti-arrhythmics to treat LQTS caused by diverse KV7.1+KCNE1 mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing N-AT effects on multiple mutants.

claim: About 80-90% of LQTS type 2-associated hERG mutants are estimated to suffer from defective trafficking.
source: Defective trafficking of mutant KV11.1 ion channels is a common cause of LQTS type 2. About 80-90% of LQTS type 2-associated hERG mutants are estimated to suffer from defective trafficking (Anderson et al., 2014; Sanguinetti, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2014 and Sanguinetti, 2010.

claim: Polyunsaturated fatty acids and their analogues (such as N-AT) attract the voltage sensor S4 in KV7.1 by an electrostatic mechanism.
source: We previously suggested that polyunsaturated fatty acids and their analogues (such as N-AT) attract the voltage sensor S4 in KV7.1 by an electrostatic mechanism and thereby shift the G(V) towards more negative voltages and speed up channel opening (Liin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liin et al., 2015.

claim: S4 moves both during the main gating charge movement and during the subsequent channel opening in KV7.1+KCNE1 channels.
source: Using voltage clamp fluorometry, we have previously shown that both the main gating charge movement and the gate opening of KV7.1+KCNE1 channels are accompanied by fluorescence signals from fluorophores attached to S4 (Barro-Soria et al., 2014). This suggests that S4 moves both during the main gating charge movement and during the subsequent channel opening in KV7.1+KCNE1 channels (Barro-Soria et al., 2014), which is similar to observations in Shaker KV channels (Börjesson and Elinder, 2011; Pathak et al., 2005; Phillips and Swartz, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barro-Soria et al., 2014; Börjesson and Elinder, 2011; Pathak et al., 2005; Phillips and Swartz, 2010.

claim: N-AT could affect both the main gating charge movement and gate opening by acting on the S4 voltage sensor.
source: Therefore, N-AT could affect both the main gating charge movement and gate opening by acting on the S4 voltage sensor, as has been shown for hanatoxin which targets the voltage-sensing domain in the Shaker KV channel (Milescu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the mechanism of hanatoxin, supported by citation to Milescu et al., 2013.

claim: There is currently no clinically approved KV7.1+KCNE1 channel activator.
source: However, there is currently no clinically approved KV7.1+KCNE1 channel activator.
evidence: This is a statement of current clinical knowledge.

claim: LQTS is today treated with drugs that prevent the triggering of arrhythmic activity, such as beta-blockers, or with arrhythmia-terminating implantable cardioverter defibrillator.
source: LQTS is today treated with drugs that prevent the triggering of arrhythmic activity, such as beta-blockers, or with arrhythmia-terminating implantable cardioverter defibrillator (Hedley et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hedley et al., 2009.

claim: In LQTS, the action potential of the heart is prolonged, which is observed as a prolonged QT interval in the electrocardiogram.
source: In LQTS, the action potential of the heart is prolonged, which is observed as a prolonged QT interval in the electrocardiogram.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LQTS.

claim: LQTS patients have an increased risk of developing ventricular tachyarrhythmias called torsades de pointes when exposed to triggers such as adrenergic stress.
source: LQTS patients have an increased risk of developing ventricular tachyarrhythmias called torsades de pointes when exposed to triggers such as adrenergic stress (Morita et al., 2008; Cerrone et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morita et al., 2008 and Cerrone et al., 2012.

claim: Torsades de pointes arrhythmias can cause palpitation, syncope or sudden death due to ventricular fibrillation.
source: These arrhythmias can cause palpitation, syncope or sudden death due to ventricular fibrillation.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about torsades de pointes.

claim: Altogether, about 300 mutations in KCNQ1 and KCNE1 have been identified in patients suffering from LQTS.
source: Altogether, about 300 mutations in KCNQ1 and KCNE1 have been identified in patients suffering from LQTS (Hedley et al., 2009) (http://www.fsm.it/cardmoc/).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hedley et al., 2009 and reference to a database.

claim: These mutations are distributed throughout the channel sequence and are therefore likely to cause channel dysfunction by different mechanisms.
source: These mutations are distributed throughout the channel sequence and are therefore likely to cause channel dysfunction by different mechanisms, which are, however, largely unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of mutations shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The mechanisms by which LQTS mutations cause channel dysfunction are largely unknown.
source: These mutations are distributed throughout the channel sequence and are therefore likely to cause channel dysfunction by different mechanisms, which are, however, largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Potential mechanisms for KV7.1+KCNE1 channel loss of function by a mutation could be interference with voltage sensor movement, gate opening, or membrane expression.
source: Potential mechanisms for KV7.1+KCNE1 channel loss of function by a mutation could, for example, be interference with voltage sensor movement, gate opening, or membrane expression.
evidence: This is a statement of potential mechanisms based on channel structure and function.

claim: KV7.1+KCNE1 channels have a relatively high Q10 of around 5–7.5.
source: The 5 s voltage pulse to +20 mV (or + 40 mV) at room temperature was chosen to make the KV7.1+KCNE1 channel activate to a similar extent as during a ventricular action potential (300–400 ms) at body temperature (note that KV7.1+KCNE1 channels have a relatively high Q10 of around 5–7.5 [Busch and Lang, 1993; Seebohm et al., 2001]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Busch and Lang, 1993 and Seebohm et al., 2001.

claim: N-AT is an interesting prototype compound that may inspire development of future IKs channel activators to treat Long QT syndrome caused by diverse IKs channel mutations.
source: N-arachidonoyl taurine is therefore an interesting prototype compound that may inspire development of future IKs channel activators to treat Long QT syndrome caused by diverse IKs channel mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing N-AT effects on multiple mutants.
